posts.style: Design & Aspiration · The Kitchen That Faces the Fire
posts.alt: A modern La Jolla backyard in late-afternoon light with a black aluminum StruXure louvered pergola with recessed downlights over a large-format porcelain terrace, a sand-toned outdoor kitchen with a stainless Lynx built-in grill and bar counter with three black barstools, a long board-formed concrete linear fire table burning in front of a built-in concrete bench, potted olive trees and agave, and a two-story white stucco contemporary home with black-framed windows
posts.hook: Most outdoor kitchens are built with their back to the party. This one isn't.
posts.caption:
Look at where the grill sits. The person cooking faces the fire table and the bench, not a wall. That single decision is what turns a kitchen into the middle of the evening instead of a job someone does on the edge of it.

Everything else follows from it. The louvered roof opens for winter sun and closes for a July afternoon, with lighting built into the blades so the room doesn't go dark at six. The linear fire table runs parallel to the bench, so the seating reads as one long conversation rather than a circle of chairs. The porcelain underfoot doesn't stain when the wine does, and the concrete, stone and stucco stay in the same quiet palette as the house.

Nothing here is loud. It's just arranged around how people actually stand, cook and linger.

The selections:
• StruXure louvered pergola with integrated downlights
• large-format porcelain pavers
• Lynx built-in grill & stainless cabinetry
• board-formed concrete linear fire table & bench
• potted olive trees & agave

See a selection you'd want in your own yard? DM “DESIGN”.

posts.alt: A San Miguel Ranch suburban backyard at dusk with a round Belgard paver fire circle around a stone gas fire pit, four cushioned wicker lounge chairs with folded throws, a wide SYNLawn artificial lawn, cedar raised planter beds with citrus trees and ornamental grasses along a wood fence, cafe string lights overhead, and two-story tile-roof homes glowing beyond
posts.hook: The best seat in the house in November is outside, about four feet from a fire.
posts.caption:
Evenings in San Diego get short this time of year, but they don't get cold enough to send you in. What they need is a reason to stay out.

This yard gives it one. A paver circle set a step away from the lawn, a gas fire that lights with a switch, and four deep chairs pulled close enough to talk without raising your voice. The lawn stays green without a sprinkler schedule, so the kids have somewhere to run while the adults don't move. Cedar planters along the fence hold citrus and grasses at eye level, and the string lights give the whole thing a ceiling once the sky goes blue.

A normal suburban lot. A very good reason to skip the couch.

The selections:
• Belgard paver fire circle
• stone-clad gas fire pit
• SYNLawn artificial turf
• cedar raised planters with citrus & ornamental grasses
• cafe string lighting

Want a yard your family actually lives in after dark? DM “DESIGN”.

posts.style: Seasonal · Veterans Day · Point Loma Curb Appeal
posts.alt: A single-story Point Loma home of stacked stone and horizontal wood siding at sunset, with a wide warm-grey herringbone paver driveway and entry court, mature olive trees, agave, blue grasses and drought-tolerant planting, warm wall sconces and low path lights leading to a wood front door
posts.hook: Today, a quiet thank you from a city built around those who served.
posts.caption:
San Diego is a Navy town, and Point Loma wears that history closer than most. Its streets run down toward the bay, past the base and the white rows of Fort Rosecrans, and plenty of the families on them have given years of service to the rest of us.

So today isn't a day for selling anything. It's a day to say thank you — to the veterans in our neighborhoods, in our clients' homes, and in our own families. We're grateful to do our work in a city you helped shape.

The front of the house is where every homecoming starts. Here it's kept simple: a wide herringbone paver court that reads as one calm surface from the street, olive trees and drought planting set back to frame the stone and wood, and low lights that walk you to the door after dark.

The selections:
• Belgard herringbone paver driveway & entry court
• stacked stone veneer facade
• mature olive trees, agave & blue grasses
• FX Luminaire path lights & wall sconces

If you're thinking about the front of your own home, DM “DESIGN” whenever you're ready.

A permeable driveway of large-format Techo-Bloc Blu 60 slab pavers in warm grey with dymondia groundcover in the joints; a matching front walk. Low board-formed concrete planter wall with an olive tree, bougainvillea on the fence, agave, lavender and ornamental grasses; a mature Torrey pine and a glimpse of San Diego Bay beyond. FX Luminaire path lights just beginning to glow. Straight level verticals, eye level, 24mm architectural lens, one dominant warm low sun from the side with real cast shadows, natural highlight rolloff, deep true shadows, shallow depth of field, fine film grain, warm neutral editorial color grade, restrained saturation. A single photograph, no collage, no split screen, no grid. No people, no humans, no faces, no text, no watermark. (4:5, 4k, then realism pass --preset editorial.) If regenerated, update the selections to: Techo-Bloc Blu 60 slab driveway with dymondia joints, board-formed concrete planter wall, olive, bougainvillea & lavender, FX Luminaire path lights.

posts.style: Craft & Process · Where the Water Goes
posts.alt: A compact North Park backyard behind a sage-green craftsman bungalow at twilight: a large-format porcelain paver courtyard, a freestanding stained cedar pergola strung with cafe lights, a dark stone water bowl on river rock, a living green wall along the fence, potted citrus trees in terracotta, and mature street trees and power lines above the neighboring roofs
posts.hook: On a small lot, water has nowhere to go but where you send it.
posts.caption:
A big yard forgives a lot. A 30-foot courtyard between a bungalow and a garage forgives nothing — get the fall wrong by a fraction and the first real rain ends up against the house.

So the part of this job you'll never notice is the part that matters most. The porcelain is set on a compacted base with a slight, deliberate pitch away from the foundation, and every surface is planned to hand its water to a drain or a planting bed before it reaches a wall. Large-format porcelain helps: fewer joints, a surface that won't absorb or stain, and a finish that stays grippy when wet. Only once the water has a path do the finishes arrive — the cedar pergola, the stone water bowl, the green wall, the citrus in terracotta.

The pretty part took a weekend to style. The grading is why it'll still look like this in ten years.

The selections:
• large-format porcelain pavers
• stained cedar pergola with cafe lighting
• Bobe-style stone water bowl on river rock
• living green wall
• potted Meyer lemon & citrus in terracotta

Working with a tight lot? DM “DESIGN” and we'll show you how we'd handle it.

posts.style: Trust & Difference · Drone Aerial · Your Address Stays Yours
posts.alt: Top-down drone aerial of a Carmel Valley backyard with a blue and grey VersaCourt half-court for basketball and pickleball framed by a light paver border, a basketball hoop on a white wall, a wide SYNLawn artificial lawn around the court, borders of agave, blue fescue and succulents, and a terracotta tile roof along the bottom edge
posts.hook: You won't find our clients' addresses on this page. That's on purpose.
posts.caption:
A lot of contractors will happily send you to drive past their last job. We won't — and we'd rather tell you why than be vague about it.

The homes we work on belong to families, not to our marketing. Nobody should find a stranger slowing down outside their house because a contractor used it as a showroom. So when you're considering working with us, you get written references and a detailed photographic record during discovery, and the people who live there get left alone. It's the same discretion we'll show your home once it's finished.

This is the kind of view you'll see from us: the whole design, top-down, and not a house number in sight. A half-court set in a clean paver frame, turf to soften every edge, and drought planting that holds the boundary without a single hedge to trim.

The selections:
• VersaCourt basketball & pickleball court tiles
• paver border & court surround
• SYNLawn artificial turf
• agave, blue fescue & succulent borders

References available on request. Want to talk through your own yard? DM “DESIGN”.
